content.content:
1	# ChronicleFlow
2	
3	ChronicleFlow is a small backend for durable workflow orchestration. It stores
4	workflow definitions, execution state, and an append-only event history in
5	SQLite so an execution can be inspected and replayed deterministically.
6	
7	The initial release intentionally supports a compact public contract:
8	
9	- workflows are directed acyclic graphs of `task`, `condition`, bounded
10	  `loop`, and dynamic `map` nodes;
11	- a workflow may declare named versions: every declared version is kept and
12	  each execution is bound to the version that was current (or explicitly
13	  named) when it started, so upgrading a workflow never changes a running
14	  execution, and a running execution can be explicitly migrated to another
15	  version of the same workflow, after which it advances under that version;
16	- executions advance one ready task at a time, evaluating conditions and
17	  skipping unmatched branches automatically;
18	- task nodes may declare a bounded number of retries: a submitted failure
19	  re-queues the node until the retries are exhausted, which terminates the
20	  execution;
21	- a task node may declare an approval point with the people allowed to decide
22	  it; advancing parks the task in a waiting state until an approver approves
23	  (completing it with the submitted output) or rejects (terminating the
24	  execution with reason `rejected`);
25	- executions may declare a timeout in seconds, after which they terminate and
26	  no longer accept output, and they may be cancelled explicitly;
27	- loop nodes repeat their body a bounded number of times, re-evaluating a
28	  continue condition at the loop boundaries;
29	- a map node inside a loop body expands independently in every iteration
30	  from that iteration's source output, its instances and events belonging
31	  to the iteration they expanded in;
32	- every state transition is appended to the execution event stream;
33	- replay rebuilds execution state from the recorded events;
34	- a checkpoint is written at every node boundary, capturing the state
35	  summary and event position, so an execution can be recovered from the
36	  latest checkpoint after a restart;
37	- workers may claim a running execution to receive a work item with a
38	  time-bounded lease, renew the lease with heartbeats, and release it;
39	  while a lease is active only its holder may submit results, and an
40	  expired or released lease returns the work item to the claimable set;
41	- duplicate commands with the same idempotency key return the original result;
42	- workflows and executions may declare webhook subscriptions, and matching
43	  business events are delivered to the declared targets with bounded retries,
44	  each delivery recorded in a per-execution history;
45	- subscriptions may also declare queue targets instead of webhook addresses:
46	  matching business events are appended, in occurrence order, to persistent
47	  per-execution queues that callers pull from and acknowledge explicitly,
48	  with a visibility timeout returning unacknowledged messages to the pending
49	  set (delivery is at least once);
50	- a workflow may declare a schedule — a fixed interval in seconds or a
51	  five-field cron plan — and the service automatically creates one execution
52	  per due period with the declared input; schedules can be paused and
53	  resumed, and periods missed while paused are either caught up once or
54	  skipped, according to the declared missed policy.
55	
56	## Requirements
57	
58	- Python 3.11 or newer
59	- no third-party runtime dependencies
60	
61	## Run the service
62	
63	```bash
64	PYTHONPATH=src python -m chronicleflow.server --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080 --database chronicleflow.db
65	```
66	
67	The process prints `ChronicleFlow listening on http://127.0.0.1:8080` after it
68	has bound the port.
69	
70	## HTTP API
71	
72	All request and response bodies are JSON. Unknown fields are rejected.
73	
74	Responses are compact JSON with no insignificant whitespace, and every
75	response body ends with exactly one trailing newline (`\n`). Numbers
76	round-trip with their full precision: finite floats keep their original
77	IEEE-754 value through the shortest textual representation that decodes to
78	it (so `0.30000000000000004` stays `0.30000000000000004`), negative zero is
79	preserved as `-0.0`, and integers stay integers. Non-finite numbers may
80	never appear in a request and are never produced in a response; timestamps
81	are ISO-8601 UTC strings ending in `Z`.
82	
83	### Tenants and quotas
84	
85	A request may declare a tenant by sending the `X-Tenant-Id` header with a
86	non-empty identifier. Every workflow, execution, schedule, schedule status,
87	delivery history, and queue record is scoped to the tenant of the request that
88	created it: queries and operations only ever see data belonging to that
89	tenant, and different tenants may use the same workflow or execution
90	identifiers without colliding. Referencing another tenant's resource — for
91	example advancing, migrating, deciding, claiming, cancelling, recovering, replaying, or
92	reading the events, checkpoints, deliveries, queues, or schedule of an execution or
93	workflow owned by another tenant, or pulling from or acknowledging one of its
94	queues — is answered exactly like a reference to a
95	missing resource: `404 not_found`, with no indication that the resource
96	exists elsewhere. An execution created in one tenant can only reference a
97	workflow of the same tenant, and a migration can only name a version of that
98	workflow in the same tenant; referencing an unseen workflow identifier or
99	version is the usual `404 not_found`.
100	
101	The header applies to every workflow, execution, and schedule entry point,
102	including creation, advancement, migration, approval decisions, lease
103	operations, cancellation, recovery, replay, instance deletion and
104	modification and re-expansion, queue pulls, acknowledgements, and all
105	history and status queries, as well as the usage, bill, and metrics queries. An empty
106	`X-Tenant-Id` value is a `400 validation_error`. Requests that omit the
107	header entirely keep using the single legacy namespace, whose advancement,
108	approvals, leases, retries, timeouts, cancellation, checkpoints, recovery,
109	scheduling, and replay behavior is byte-for-byte unchanged: the tenant is
110	stored only as database scope, never added to a state field or event payload,
111	and state shapes and event streams gain no new fields. Idempotency keys are
112	scoped per tenant as well, so tenants can never see or collide with each
113	other's keys; reusing a key for another operation within the same tenant is
114	the usual `409 conflict`.
115	
116	A tenant may declare quotas bounding how many workflows and executions it may
117	hold:
118	
119	```http
120	PUT /quotas
121	Idempotency-Key: quota-request-1
122	X-Tenant-Id: acme
123	
124	{"workflows": 10, "executions": 100}
125	```
126	
127	`POST` to the same path is accepted as well. The body must contain exactly
128	`workflows` and `executions`, each a positive integer; a non-positive,
129	non-integer, boolean, or non-finite value, a missing or extra field, or a
130	non-object body is a `400 validation_error` that writes nothing. Both quota
131	routes require a tenant: calling them without `X-Tenant-Id` (or with an empty
132	one) is a `400 validation_error`. The response is
133	`{"quota":{"workflows":10,"executions":100}}`; declaring again replaces the
134	limits (re-anchoring nothing else). Lowering a limit below the current
135	holding deletes no existing data — existing workflows and executions stay
136	fully usable — it only rejects later writes that would exceed the new limit.
137	
138	```http
139	GET /quotas
140	X-Tenant-Id: acme
141	```
142	
143	Returns the declared quota, or the definite empty result `{"quota":null}`
144	when the tenant has declared none.
145	
146	When a write would take the tenant past either limit, the whole request is
147	rejected with `409 conflict` and an error message that names the quota (for
148	example `quota exceeded: tenant already holds 10 workflows (quota limit is
149	10)`), so callers can tell quota rejection apart from an ordinary identifier
150	conflict. The rejection performs no partial write: nothing is inserted and
151	previously stored data is unaffected, exactly as for validation failures.
152	
153	A schedule firing on time creates its execution in the schedule's tenant and
154	that execution counts against the tenant's execution quota. When the tenant
155	is at its execution limit, the due period creates no execution and the
156	schedule is left unchanged — its cursor, `last_triggered_at`, and
157	`last_execution_id` stay as they were — so the period is settled on a later
158	pass once capacity exists, under the usual per-period idempotence. Delivery
159	history follows the tenant of the execution it belongs to.
160	
161	### Usage metering and billing
162	
163	Requests that carry a tenant identifier leave a usage record for each billable
164	action they perform. Only tenant-scoped requests are metered: a request that
165	omits the `X-Tenant-Id` header keeps the legacy namespace and writes no usage
166	record at all, with its state shapes and event content unchanged. The four
167	metered action types are:
168	
169	- `workflow_created` — a workflow definition is stored. Adding a new version
170	  to an existing workflow is one workflow creation, the same as the first
171	  definition;
172	- `execution_started` — an execution is created and starts `running`;
173	- `schedule_triggered` — a due schedule period creates its execution. The
174	  scheduled execution is metered both as `execution_started` and as
175	  `schedule_triggered`;
176	- `delivery_attempted` — one outbound webhook HTTP attempt is made, or one
177	  queue message is delivered to a caller pulling from a queue. A
178	  subscription that retries is metered once per attempt, so a delivery that
179	  fails and then succeeds on its second attempt records two attempts; the
180	  action is metered whether it ultimately succeeds or fails. A queue pull
181	  meters one attempt per message it delivers, so a redelivery after the
182	  visibility timeout is metered again, while a pull that delivers nothing
183	  meters nothing.
184	
185	Metering is atomic with the action it describes: a write rejected by
186	validation or by a quota produces no record and performs no partial write.
187	Repeating an idempotent command returns its first result and writes no second
188	record, and settling the same schedule period more than once (a repeated
189	trigger or a later pass) meters that period only once. Replay, recovery, and
190	queries never meter and never alter recorded usage or billing conclusions.
191	
192	```http
193	GET /usage
194	X-Tenant-Id: acme
195	```
196	
197	Returns `{"usage":[{"type":"execution_started","count":1}, ...]}`: the
198	cumulative count of recorded actions per type, sorted by ascending type
199	identifier. Types with no records are omitted, so a tenant with no usage gets
200	the definite empty result `{"usage":[]}`.
201	
202	```http
203	GET /bill
204	X-Tenant-Id: acme
205	```
206	
207	Returns the per-type bill:
208	
209	```json
210	{"bill":{"items":[
211	  {"type":"execution_started","count":1,"unit_price":100,"subtotal":100},
212	  {"type":"workflow_created","count":2,"unit_price":1000,"subtotal":2000}
213	],"total":2100}}
214	```
215	
216	Each item gives the metered `count`, a positive-integer `unit_price` in cents
217	that is also returned in the response, and a `subtotal` equal to
218	`count * unit_price`; `total` is the integer-cent sum of every subtotal. With
219	no records, `items` is empty and `total` is `0`.
220	
221	Both endpoints are tenant-scoped `GET` requests: a missing or empty
222	`X-Tenant-Id` is a `400 validation_error`. Usage and bill data follow the
223	usual tenant isolation, so one tenant can never see another's records.
224	
225	### Operational metrics
226	
227	```http
228	GET /metrics
229	X-Tenant-Id: acme
230	```
231	
232	Returns one line of compact JSON summarizing the business facts already
233	recorded for the tenant, ending with the usual single newline. The endpoint
234	is read-only: it appends no events, writes no usage records, and changes no
235	stored data, and it reports only persisted facts — it performs no
236	advancement, approval, recovery, or replay of its own, so those operations
237	never change what a metrics query observes beyond the facts they themselves
238	recorded. A missing or empty `X-Tenant-Id` is a `400 validation_error`, and
239	the metrics follow the usual tenant isolation: another tenant's facts are
240	never visible in any dimension and never affect this tenant's counts. A
241	tenant with no recorded facts at all gets the definite empty result with
242	every dimension at zero — not an error. With no query parameters the answer
243	is every fact recorded for the tenant, byte for byte.
244	
245	The query accepts two optional query parameters, each an ISO-8601 UTC
246	timestamp ending in `Z`:
247	
248	```http
249	GET /metrics?since=2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-26T09:00:00.000Z
250	X-Tenant-Id: acme
251	```
252	
253	- `since` and `until` bound a **closed** interval on the facts' occurrence
254	  times: a fact whose time equals `since` or `until` is counted. When either
255	  parameter is absent the corresponding bound is open, so omitting both
256	  counts every recorded fact;
257	- a malformed `since` or `until`, a repeated parameter, or any unknown query
258	  parameter is a `400 validation_error`;
259	- when `since` is later than `until` the request is not an error: the window
260	  simply contains no facts, so every dimension reports its definite zero
261	  result.
262	
263	Each dimension is windowed by the occurrence time of its own fact: node
264	completions, failures, and retry consumption use the time of their recorded
265	node events; delivery outcomes use the delivery record's `occurred_at`
266	(shared by every attempt recorded in it); schedule triggers use the settled
267	period's trigger time; and the status distribution counts an execution at
268	the time it entered its current status — a still-running execution at its
269	start time, and a completed or terminated execution at the time of its
270	completion or termination event.
271	
272	### Export metrics in Prometheus text format
273	
274	```http
275	GET /metrics/export
276	X-Tenant-Id: acme
277	```
278	
279	A read-only tenant-scoped entry point that returns the same counts as the
280	metrics query — including the same optional `since` and `until` filters, the
281	same closed-interval semantics, the same definite zero result for a window
282	with `since` later than `until`, and the same `400 validation_error` for a
283	missing or empty tenant, a malformed timestamp, or an unknown query
284	parameter — rendered in the Prometheus text exposition format
285	(`text/plain; version=0.0.4`). It writes no events and no usage records.
286	
287	Each top-level metrics dimension is one metric family named with the
288	dimension's public key prefixed by `chronicleflow_`. The families appear in
289	the documented top-level key order, and the samples within a family are
290	ordered by ascending label value:
291	
292	- `chronicleflow_status_distribution` — samples carry a `status` label
293	  (`running`, `completed`, `terminated`); only the terminated samples also
294	  carry a `reason` label naming one of the four termination reasons;
295	- `chronicleflow_node_completions`, `chronicleflow_node_failures`, and
296	  `chronicleflow_retry_consumption` — samples carry a `node` label;
297	- `chronicleflow_schedule_triggers` — samples carry a `workflow` label;
298	- `chronicleflow_delivery_succeeded` and `chronicleflow_delivery_failed` —
299	  unlabeled scalar samples.
300	
301	Every value is a decimal integer. A dimension with no facts in the window
302	still exposes a zero-valued sample line (the labeled families expose one
303	unlabeled `0` sample). Every line ends with a newline and the whole document
304	ends with a single newline.
305	
306	The top-level keys appear in this order — status distribution, node
307	completions, node failures, retry consumption, delivery successes, delivery
308	failures, and schedule triggers:
309	
310	```json
311	{"status_distribution":{"running":1,"completed":2,"terminated":{"cancelled":0,"rejected":1,"retries_exhausted":0,"timeout":0}},"node_completions":{"charge":3},"node_failures":{"charge":2},"retry_consumption":{"charge":1},"delivery_succeeded":4,"delivery_failed":1,"schedule_triggers":{"nightly-orders":2}}
312	```
313	
314	- `status_distribution` — the tenant's executions divided into `running`,
315	  `completed`, and `terminated`; `terminated` is further broken down by
316	  termination reason, with every reason (`cancelled`, `rejected`,
317	  `retries_exhausted`, `timeout`) always present, zero when no execution
318	  ended for that reason.
319	- `node_completions` — persisted node completion facts per node identifier.
320	  Condition evaluations and skips are not completions and are never counted;
321	  a loop body node counts once per iteration it completes.
322	- `node_failures` — submitted task failures per node identifier; a loop body
323	  node accumulates each iteration's failures.
324	- `retry_consumption` — the number of times a failed task was re-queued for
325	  another attempt, per node identifier.
326	- `delivery_succeeded` and `delivery_failed` — outbound delivery attempts by
327	  outcome. Every attempt counts exactly once, so a delivery that fails and
328	  then succeeds on a later attempt records one of each.
329	- `schedule_triggers` — schedule periods that created an execution, per
330	  workflow identifier; settling the same period again counts nothing more.
331	
332	All counts are non-negative integers. A dimension with no facts reports zero
333	(or an empty group) rather than being omitted, and the groups within a
334	dimension are ordered by ascending identifier. Migrating an execution to
335	another version does not change attribution: facts recorded before and after
336	the migration accumulate under the same names. The optional `since` and
337	`until` filters and the Prometheus text export are described above.
338	
339	### Health
340	
341	```http
342	GET /health
343	```
344	
345	Returns `{"status":"ok"}`.
346	
347	### Create a workflow
348	
349	```http
350	POST /workflows
351	Idempotency-Key: workflow-request-1
352	
353	{
354	  "id": "order-flow",
355	  "nodes": [
356	    {"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []},
357	    {"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"]}
358	  ]
359	}
360	```
361	
362	Returns HTTP 201 with the stored workflow. Node identifiers must be unique,
363	dependencies must exist, and cycles are rejected.
364	
365	A workflow definition may carry an optional `version` tag; declaring one
366	enables upgrades and keeps every version. Versioning is described under
367	"Workflow versions" below, and a workflow's stored versions and current
368	version are available through `GET /workflows/{id}`.
369	
370	A workflow may also declare webhook `subscriptions` alongside its nodes:
371	
372	```json
373	{
374	  "id": "order-flow",
375	  "nodes": [{"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []}],
376	  "subscriptions": [{"url": "https://hooks.example.com/orders", "events": ["execution_completed"]}]
377	}
378	```
379	
380	See "Webhook notifications" below for the subscription shape and delivery
381	semantics; the subscriptions apply to every execution of the workflow (for a
382	versioned workflow, to executions bound to that version).
383	
384	A workflow may also declare a `schedule` alongside its nodes:
385	
386	```json
387	{
388	  "id": "nightly-orders",
389	  "nodes": [{"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []}],
390	  "schedule": {"interval_seconds": 3600, "input": {"mode": "nightly"}, "missed_policy": "catch_up"}
391	}
392	```
393	
394	See "Schedules" below for the declaration shape and the trigger semantics.
395	
396	Besides `task`, a node may have `kind` set to `condition`:
397	
398	```json
399	{"id": "is_vip", "kind": "condition", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "path": "customer.vip", "equals": true}
400	```
401	
402	`path` is a non-empty dot-separated path into the execution input and `equals`
403	is a JSON scalar (string, number, boolean, or null). A condition is evaluated
404	automatically once its dependencies complete: the input value at `path` is
405	compared with `equals` by JSON type and value, and a missing path evaluates to
406	`false`.
407	
408	A task may carry an optional `run_if` guard:
409	
410	```json
411	{"id": "expedite", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["is_vip"], "run_if": {"condition_id": "is_vip", "expected": true}}
412	```
413	
414	`condition_id` must reference a `condition` node that is also listed in the
415	task's `depends_on`. When the condition's result differs from `expected`, the
416	task is marked as skipped: it receives no output and still satisfies the
417	dependencies of its successors.
418	
419	A task may declare how many times it is retried after a failure:
420	
421	```json
422	{"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "retries": 3}
423	```
424	
425	`retries` is an integer between 0 and 10 and defaults to 0, meaning the task
426	is attempted only once. Each failure submitted through `advance` consumes one
427	attempt; while retries remain, the task returns to the ready set and is
428	advanced again. When a failure arrives with no retries left, the task is
429	permanently failed and the whole execution terminates with termination reason
430	`retries_exhausted`.
431	
432	A task may instead declare an approval point:
433	
434	```json
435	{"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "approval": {"approvers": ["alice", "bob"]}}
436	```
437	
438	`approval` contains exactly `approvers`, a non-empty array of approver
439	identifier strings without duplicates; an empty list, a duplicate entry, or a
440	non-string entry is a validation error, and only `task` nodes may carry an
441	approval point. When an `advance` reaches a ready task with an approval point,
442	the task does not complete and the submitted output or failure is not
443	consumed: an `approval_requested` event is appended (recording the node, its
444	approvers, and, inside a loop body, the loop id and iteration) and the
445	execution stays `running`, parked in a waiting state returned under
446	`waiting_approval`. Further `advance` calls return the current state without
447	writing output, completing the node, or appending events; only a decision can
448	move the task.
449	
450	### Submit an approval decision
451	
452	```http
453	POST /executions/run-1/decision
454	Idempotency-Key: decision-request-1
455	
456	{"approver":"alice","decision":"approved","output":{"charge_id":"c-3"}}
457	```
458	
459	`decision` is either `approved` or `rejected`. An approved decision carries
460	exactly `approver`, `decision`, and an `output` object; the task completes with
461	that output and its successors become available in the usual way. A rejected
462	decision carries exactly `approver`, `decision`, and a `reason` string; the
463	task is permanently failed (it is listed under `failed_nodes`) and the
464	execution terminates with termination reason `rejected`. Either decision
465	appends an `approval_decided` event with the node, approver, decision, and (on
466	rejection) the reason, and the approval record is kept under `approvals`. A
467	request whose approver is not in the point's approver list is a 409
468	`conflict`, and a malformed body or a decision value other than `approved` or
469	`rejected` is a 400 `validation_error`; neither changes execution state.
470	Repeating the decision that already resolved the most recent approval point —
471	the same approver and decision with the same output or rejection reason —
472	returns the first result and neither advances the node again nor appends
473	another event; any other decision against an execution with no pending
474	approval point is a 409 `conflict`, and deciding a missing execution returns
475	404.
476	
477	While an execution is parked at an approval point it remains `running`, so a
478	cancellation takes effect immediately with the usual `cancelled` termination
479	reason, and a reached timeout terminates it with `timeout`; both dismiss the
480	pending point and the execution then no longer accepts decisions or output.
481	The waiting point, its request and decision events, and the termination
482	reason are rebuilt solely from the event stream on replay, and the parked and
483	decided node boundaries are checkpointed like every other boundary, so
484	waiting points and recorded decisions remain valid after a restart. Approval
485	state is added to an execution only when its workflow declares at least one
486	approval point; workflows without approvals keep exactly the previous state
487	shape and event stream.
488	
489	A node may also have `kind` set to `loop`, describing a bounded repeated
490	segment:
491	
492	```json
493	{"id": "retry", "kind": "loop", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "entry": "attempt", "condition": "keep_trying", "max_iterations": 3}
494	```
495	
496	A loop node contains exactly `id`, `kind`, `depends_on`, `entry`, `condition`,
497	and `max_iterations`; any other field is rejected as unknown. `entry` names a
498	`task` node, `condition` names a `condition` node, and `max_iterations` is an
499	integer between 1 and 100. The loop body is the repeated segment anchored by
500	the entry task and the condition: it is the entry task, the condition, and
501	every node either anchor reaches through `depends_on`. The two anchors must
502	be connected — the condition gates the entry task (the entry depends on it)
503	or the condition is evaluated after the entry task (it depends on the entry),
504	as in the example above. The body keeps the usual DAG rules and always
505	contains the referenced condition. The loop's own dependencies must be
506	completed or skipped before the first iteration may start, they must not
507	overlap the body, bodies of different loops must not overlap or nest, and
508	nodes outside a body must not depend on nodes inside it (they depend on the
509	loop node instead).
510	
511	When the loop's dependencies are satisfied, the loop evaluates its condition
512	against the execution input (same JSON type and value comparison as condition
513	nodes; a missing path is `false`). If it is `false`, the loop completes with
514	zero iterations and end reason `condition_false`. If it is `true`, the first
515	iteration starts and the body advances one ready task per `advance` call in
516	the usual deterministic order; conditions and `run_if` skips inside the body
517	are re-evaluated every iteration, and task outputs belong only to the current
518	iteration. Once every body node is completed or skipped, the condition is
519	evaluated again: `true` starts the next iteration, `false` ends the loop with
520	`condition_false`, and reaching `max_iterations` ends it with
521	`iteration_limit` after that iteration finishes. Ending the loop completes
522	the loop node and releases the dependencies of its successors. Once the loop
523	has finished, the execution-level `completed_nodes` list also includes every
524	body node that completed in any iteration, each listed only once and in the
525	order of its first completion, followed by the loop node itself; body nodes
526	skipped by a `run_if` guard remain out of the execution-level completed list
527	and are visible only in their iteration record. Body task outputs still
528	belong only to their iterations.
529	
530	Execution state exposes each loop under `loops`: `status`, the
531	`current_iteration`, one entry per iteration with its own `completed_nodes`,
532	`skipped_nodes`, `condition_results`, and `outputs`, and the single
533	`end_reason` (`condition_false` or `iteration_limit`). The event stream
534	records `iteration_started`, `loop_condition_evaluated`, and `loop_completed`
535	events alongside the usual per-node ones, so replay rebuilds loop state
536	exactly.
537	
538	### Dynamic map nodes
539	
540	A `map` node expands at runtime into one task instance per element of a
541	recorded array:
542	
543	```json
544	{"id": "ship", "kind": "map", "depends_on": ["collect"],
545	 "source": "collect", "path": "items", "max_instances": 100,
546	 "template": {"id": "ship-item", "retries": 2}}
547	```
548	
549	A map node contains exactly `id`, `kind`, `depends_on`, `source`, `path`,
550	`max_instances`, and `template`; any other field is rejected as unknown.
551	
552	- `source` names a `task` node that is also listed in `depends_on`. Expansion
553	  begins only after every dependency has completed or been skipped; the
554	  element list comes solely from the source task's recorded output.
555	- `path` is a non-empty dot-separated path into that recorded output, using
556	  the same path syntax as a condition.
557	- `max_instances` is a positive integer bounding how many elements may
558	  expand.
559	- `template` describes the single task each instance runs and contains
560	  exactly an `id`, and optionally `retries` (an integer between 0 and 10,
561	  defaulting to 0) and an `approval` point with the same shape a task node
562	  uses. The template id only names the dynamically expanded instances; it
563	  may coincide with a declared node id or with another map's template id.
564	  A map node may also sit inside a loop body, expanding independently in
565	  every iteration (see "Maps inside loop bodies" below).
566	
567	When the dependencies settle, the value at `path` is read once. When it is an
568	array, one instance is created per element; the instances queue in ascending
569	element index order. Each `advance` still settles exactly one ready item, so
570	instances are worked in index order, one per call. An instance is an ordinary
571	task in every other respect: a submitted failure consumes the template's
572	retry bound and re-queues that instance, and a template approval point parks
573	the execution with the instance's `map_id` and `index` recorded, until an
574	approver decides it. Retries and approvals are per instance: results never
575	overwrite another instance.
576	
577	When every instance is completed, the map node completes and its output,
578	recorded both in the node's `outputs` entry and under its `maps` record, is
579	the list of instance outputs in ascending element order; its successors then
580	become available in the usual way.
581	
582	A value that is missing or is not an array expands to zero instances: the map
583	completes with an empty output list and releases its successors immediately.
584	When the array holds more elements than `max_instances`, no instance is
585	created at all: the map node fails permanently, is listed under
586	`failed_nodes`, and the execution terminates with reason `retries_exhausted`
587	under the usual exhaustion semantics.
588	
589	Execution state exposes each map under `maps`: the node's `status`
590	(`pending`, `running`, `completed`, or `failed`), one record per retained
591	instance giving its `index`, `status` (`ready`, `waiting`, `completed`, or
592	`failed`), its `output`, and its `failure_reason` (null except for a
593	permanently failed instance), plus the ordered completed `outputs` list and
594	the node's single `failure_reason`. A `ready` instance that has been
595	rewritten by a successful modify additionally carries that rewritten
596	`input`; every other instance record keeps exactly these fields. The `maps`
597	field is present only when the bound workflow declares a map node outside
598	any loop body; every other execution keeps its previous state shape.
599	
600	The event stream records a `map_expanded` event when expansion happens,
601	carrying the map id and the number of created instances (zero for a missing
602	or non-array value, and zero together with `exceeded` and the observed
603	element count when the bound is exceeded), and a `map_completed` event with
604	the map id and final instance count. Each instance's per-node events —
605	`node_completed`, `node_failed`, and `node_retried`, plus
606	`approval_requested` and `approval_decided` for a template approval point —
607	carry their `map_id` and element `index` alongside the template node id, so
608	replay rebuilds every instance solely from the event stream. Checkpoints are
609	written at instance boundaries, so recovery resumes with the unfinished
610	instances and never repeats an instance output. Per-instance completions and
611	failures count toward the existing node metrics under the template node id,
612	and webhook and queue subscriptions receive instance events exactly like any
613	other node event. Instance deletion and modification add their own
614	`instance_deleted` and `instance_modified` events, and re-expansion adds a
615	`map_reexpanded` event, described under
616	"Delete and modify expanded instances" below.
617	
618	### Maps inside loop bodies
619	
620	A map node may belong to a loop body — it is part of the body exactly when
621	the loop's entry or condition reaches it through `depends_on`, like any
622	other body member:
623	
624	```json
625	{"id": "fanout", "kind": "map", "depends_on": ["attempt"],
626	 "source": "attempt", "path": "items", "max_instances": 10,
627	 "template": {"id": "work", "retries": 1}}
628	```
629	
630	A nested map expands once per iteration, when every dependency of its node
631	is completed or skipped in that iteration, and the element list is read from
632	the source task's output of that same iteration. The expansion rules are the
633	ones of an execution-level map: a missing path or a non-array value expands
634	to zero instances and the map completes for that iteration with an empty
635	output list, so the loop boundary is evaluated as usual; an element count
636	beyond `max_instances` creates no instance at all — the map fails
637	permanently, is listed under `failed_nodes`, and the execution terminates
638	with reason `retries_exhausted` under the usual exhaustion semantics.
639	
640	The expanded instances belong to their iteration only: they queue in
641	ascending element index order and are settled one per `advance`, exactly
642	like execution-level instances, and one iteration's instances never
643	overwrite another iteration's results. An instance is an ordinary task in
644	every other respect — a submitted failure consumes the template's retry
645	bound and re-queues that instance within its iteration, and a template
646	approval point parks the execution until an approver decides it — with no
647	influence from the iteration number.
648	
649	Iteration state exposes each nested map under the iteration record's `maps`
650	field, with the same per-map shape as an execution-level map (`status`, one
651	record per instance, the ordered completed `outputs`, and `failure_reason`);
652	the field is present on every iteration of a loop whose body declares a map
653	node. When a nested map completes, its node enters the iteration's
654	`completed_nodes` and its output list is recorded in the iteration's
655	`outputs`; when the loop finishes, the usual roll-up lists the map node once
656	in the execution-level `completed_nodes`, while its outputs stay with their
657	iterations. An execution-level `maps` field is not created for nested maps.
658	
659	Every event a nested expansion records carries the owning `loop_id` and
660	`iteration` alongside the map id and, for per-instance events, the element
661	`index`: `map_expanded`, `map_completed`, the per-instance `node_completed`,
662	`node_failed`, and `node_retried`, and `approval_requested` and
663	`approval_decided` for a template approval point. The `iteration_started`
664	event of a loop whose body declares map nodes carries the iteration's
665	initial `maps` skeleton, so replay rebuilds every iteration's instance list,
666	status, and ownership solely from the event stream, consistent with the
667	materialized state. Checkpoints are written at each iteration's instance
668	boundaries, so recovery continues the current iteration's unfinished
669	instances and never repeats an instance output. Cancellation, timeouts,
670	leases, retries, and approvals keep their existing semantics, and a nested
671	map never changes an execution's termination reason.
672	
673	Executions whose workflows declare no nested map behave exactly as before:
674	state fields, event contents, and advancement results are unchanged.
675	
676	### Delete and modify expanded instances
677	
678	An expanded dynamic node offers, alongside expansion and per-instance
679	advancement, two instance-level operations and a node-level re-expansion.
680	All three are ordinary idempotent HTTP commands over the same entry points
681	the rest of the service uses; they introduce no second protocol.
682	
683	An instance that has never advanced can be removed, and so can an instance
684	that has permanently failed:
685	
686	```http
687	POST /executions/run-1/maps/ship/instances/2/delete
688	Idempotency-Key: delete-instance-2
689	
690	{}
691	```
692	
693	The body must be an empty object. Removing an instance drops only that
694	instance's record: every retained instance keeps its element index, its
695	place in the queue, and its advancement order. When the removed instance was
696	the map's last unfinished instance, the node completes under the existing
697	rules with an output list containing only the retained instances' outputs,
698	in ascending element-index order, and its successors unlock as usual. An
699	instance that is waiting on an approval, or has already completed, can never
700	be deleted; attempting it returns `409 conflict` and changes no state. A
701	permanently failed instance is removable after the execution has terminated,
702	but removing it never revives the execution, alters its termination reason,
703	or changes the node's failed conclusion. When every retained instance of a
704	map inside a loop body has ended, the iteration's other nodes advance as
705	usual and the node completes or ends under the existing rules; deleting an
706	instance in one iteration never touches another iteration.
707	
708	An instance that has never advanced can also have its input rewritten
709	before it is worked:
710	
711	```http
712	POST /executions/run-1/maps/ship/instances/1/modify
713	Idempotency-Key: modify-instance-1
714	
715	{"input":{"address":"742 Evergreen Terrace"}}
716	```
717	
718	The body must contain exactly `input`, an object with the new content; it is
719	validated like every other request body (finite numbers only). The rewrite
720	changes only the parameters used when that one instance is later advanced:
721	it affects no other instance, and the output and history of an instance that
722	has already advanced (waiting, completed, or permanently failed) are
723	immutable — modifying such an instance returns `409 conflict` and changes no
724	state. The rewritten input, including its full float precision and `-0.0`,
725	is stored verbatim.
726	
727	Delete and modify calls on the same instance settle in call order: every
728	call applies to the instance list exactly as the earlier calls left it, and
729	several calls on one instance each take effect independently, one after
730	another. A rewritten instance has still never advanced, so it remains
731	deletable; deleting or modifying an instance an earlier call already
732	removed is a `404 not_found`; and a second rewrite of the same instance
733	records the first rewrite's content as its `before`.
734	
735	Both commands apply to a map nested in a loop body exactly as to an
736	execution-level map: the current running iteration's instances are
737	addressed by the same path, and every event they append carries the owning
738	`loop_id` and `iteration` alongside the map id; an execution-level instance
739	carries no loop context.
740	
741	An out-of-bounds element index, a reference to a node that is not a dynamic
742	`map`, a missing execution, or a cross-tenant reference is a `404 not_found`
743	and writes nothing. A missing or mistyped field, a non-object modify
744	`input`, an unknown field, or a non-finite number is a `400 validation_error`
745	with no partial write. Reusing an idempotency key for another operation is a
746	`409 conflict`; repeating the same command with the same key returns the
747	first result and appends no second event.
748	
749	Every successful call appends exactly one event to the execution stream:
750	
751	- an `instance_deleted` event records the action type, the owning dynamic
752	  node under `map_id`, the removed instance's element `index` and `status`
753	  (`ready` or `failed`), and, for a map inside a loop body, the `loop_id`
754	  and `iteration`;
755	- an `instance_modified` event records the action type, the owning
756	  `map_id`, the instance `index`, the content `before` the rewrite (`null`
757	  for an instance that had never been rewritten) and `after` it, and the
758	  same loop context when the instance belongs to an iteration.
759	
760	Replay rebuilds the instance list, every instance's status and ownership,
761	and each rewrite solely from the event stream: a delete drops the recorded
762	instance (and the subsequent `map_completed`, when the deletion finished the
763	node, completes it with the retained outputs), and a modify applies the
764	rewritten input to that one instance, so the rebuilt state is exactly the
765	materialized state. A checkpoint is written at the instance boundary of
766	every successful delete or modify; after a restart recovery continues the
767	unfinished instances, repeats no instance output, and never resurrects a
768	deleted instance. The operations change no advancement conclusion or
769	termination semantics: cancellation, timeouts, approvals, leases, retries,
770	and retry exhaustion keep their existing behavior. Executions that never
771	use deletion, modification, or re-expansion keep exactly their current
772	state fields, event contents, and advancement results.
773	
774	### Re-expand a dynamic node
775	
776	A dynamic node that has already expanded can be expanded again on demand —
777	above all to regenerate its instance list after deletions:
778	
779	```http
780	POST /executions/run-1/maps/ship/reexpand
781	Idempotency-Key: reexpand-1
782	
783	{}
784	```
785	
786	(The same operation is also accepted at `.../maps/ship/expand`.) The body
787	must be an empty object. Re-expansion reads the element list again from the
788	source task's recorded output — the same recorded output the first
789	expansion read, which never changes once recorded — and regenerates the
790	instance list from it: every previous instance record is replaced, and the
791	fresh instances queue from element index zero in ascending order. The
792	regenerated instances are ordinary instances in every respect: they are
793	deleted, modified, advanced, retried, and approved through the same entries
794	and with exactly the same behavior as a first expansion, and their retry
795	bounds start from zero.
796	
797	Every successful call appends exactly one `map_reexpanded` event, recording
798	the action type, the owning dynamic node under `map_id`, and the number of
799	generated instances under `instance_count`; for a map inside a loop body
800	the event also carries the owning `loop_id` and `iteration`, and only the
801	current running iteration's expansion is replaced. A node that had
802	completed returns to `running`: it leaves `completed_nodes`, its recorded
803	output entry is discarded, and when the regenerated instances have all
804	completed the node completes again under the existing rules, its result
805	list holding only the finally retained instances' outputs in ascending
806	element-index order. An empty element list completes the node again at
807	once with an empty output list, exactly like a zero-element first
808	expansion.
809	
810	Re-expansion is rejected with `409 conflict` and writes nothing when the
811	node has not expanded yet, when it has permanently failed, when one of its
812	instances is waiting on an approval decision, when the execution has
813	already completed, or when a nested map's loop is not currently running.
814	A terminated execution's unfinished node may still be re-expanded; doing so
815	never revives the execution or alters its termination reason. A missing
816	execution, a reference to a node that is not a dynamic `map`, or a
817	cross-tenant reference is a `404 not_found` and writes nothing. A
818	non-empty or non-object body, an unknown field, or a non-finite number is a
819	`400 validation_error` with no partial write. Reusing an idempotency key
820	from another operation is a `409 conflict`; repeating the same call with
821	the same key returns the first result and appends no second event. Replay
822	rebuilds the regenerated instance list, statuses, and ownership solely
823	from the event stream, a checkpoint is written at the re-expansion
824	boundary, and recovery after a restart continues the unfinished
825	regenerated instances — repeating no instance output and never resurrecting
826	an instance that stayed deleted.
827	
828	### Workflow versions
829	
830	A workflow can declare a version tag alongside its nodes:
831	
832	```json
833	{
834	  "id": "order-flow",
835	  "version": "2026-09-25",
836	  "nodes": [
837	    {"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []},
838	    {"id": "ship", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"]}
839	  ]
840	}
841	```
842	
843	`version` is an optional non-empty string of at most 100 characters, validated
844	like every other identifier. Posting it when the workflow does not yet exist
845	creates the workflow with that version; posting another definition with a new
846	`version` to the same `id` adds a new version without touching the previous
847	ones — the workflow keeps its entire history, and every stored version remains
848	usable. The most recently added version becomes the workflow's current
849	version. Posting a definition without a `version` to an existing workflow
850	still conflicts, and reusing a version tag already stored for the same
851	workflow is a `409 conflict`; either rejection writes nothing.
852	
853	A version declaration may also carry `subscriptions` and a `schedule`,
854	validated exactly like at creation. Subscriptions are attached to the
855	declared version and apply only to executions bound to it; a version without
856	subscriptions replaces none, and other versions' subscriptions stay intact.
857	Declaring a `schedule` on an added version replaces the workflow's single
858	schedule plan in the usual way (re-anchored, pause flag kept).
859	
860	An execution created without an explicit `version` binds to the workflow's
861	current version at the moment it starts:
862	
863	```http
864	POST /executions
865	Idempotency-Key: execution-versioned
866	
867	{"id":"run-v2","workflow_id":"order-flow","input":{}}
868	```
869	
870	An execution may instead name the version it wants:
871	
872	```json
873	{"id":"run-v1","workflow_id":"order-flow","version":"2026-08-01","input":{}}
874	```
875	
876	Naming a version that does not exist for the workflow is a missing-resource
877	`404 not_found`, exactly like naming a workflow that does not exist; the
878	execution is not created. Everything about an execution follows its bound
879	version: ready-node selection, condition evaluation, loop rounds, approval
880	points, retry counts, leases, and the subscriptions that fire for its events.
881	Adding a new version never interrupts an execution already running: an
882	execution started before the upgrade keeps advancing on its old version to
883	completion or termination. Its checkpoints are snapshots of the same state,
884	recovery rebuilds from the bound version, and replay rebuilds state and the
885	version binding solely from its event stream; recorded events and historical
886	conclusions never change.
887	
888	A versioned execution's state carries its `version` tag, and its
889	`execution_started` event records the same tag; querying it therefore shows
890	which version it is bound to. A workflow that never declares a version, and an
891	execution of one, keep exactly the previous behavior, state shape, and event
892	stream with no added field.
893	
894	The definition query lists every version and the current one:
895	
896	```http
897	GET /workflows/order-flow
898	```
899	
900	```json
901	{"current_version":"2026-09-25","id":"order-flow","versions":[
902	  {"id":"order-flow","nodes":[...],"version":"2026-08-01"},
903	  {"id":"order-flow","nodes":[...],"version":"2026-09-25"}
904	]}
905	```
906	
907	Versions are returned in declaration order; each entry is the stored
908	definition with its `version` tag. A workflow that never declared a version
909	returns a single untagged entry and `current_version: null`. A missing
910	workflow returns 404 `not_found`. Cross-tenant references are missing
911	resources as usual.
912	
913	### Migrate a running execution to another version
914	
915	```http
916	POST /executions/run-v1/migrate
917	Idempotency-Key: migrate-request-1
918	
919	{"version":"2026-09-25"}
920	```
921	
922	A running execution can be explicitly moved to another declared version of
923	the same workflow; after the call it keeps advancing under the new version.
924	The body must contain exactly `version`, a non-empty version identifier that
925	names a stored version of the execution's workflow. On success a
926	`version_migrated` event is appended to the event stream — it records the
927	`from_version`, the `to_version`, and the structural skeleton of the target
928	revision (its `loops`, and, when it declares approval points, its
929	`waiting_approval` and `approvals` fields) — and a checkpoint of the rebound
930	state is written at that same node boundary. The execution's state then
931	carries the target version.
932	
933	Everything that follows uses the target version's definition: ready-node
934	selection, condition evaluation, loop rounds, approval points, retries, and
935	the workflow subscriptions that fire for later events. Everything recorded
936	before the migration is kept exactly as-is: prior events, node outputs,
937	condition conclusions, and per-iteration history are never rewritten. Loops
938	introduced by the target definition begin in their initial pending state; a
939	loop the old definition knew keeps its recorded iterations and conclusion.
940	Replay rebuilds the migration point and version binding solely from the
941	event stream, and after a restart recovery continues on the migrated version
942	from the migration checkpoint, so checkpoints and materialized state agree.
943	
944	An execution parked at an approval point may also be migrated: the waiting
945	point keeps its recorded node and approver list unchanged (only a recorded
946	approver may still decide it), and once the decision lands the subsequent
947	advancement follows the target version. Executions that are never migrated
948	keep advancing on the version they started with to completion or
949	termination; adding versions never moves them. An execution of a workflow
950	that never declared a version cannot name a target, and such workflows and
951	their executions keep exactly the previous behavior, state shape, and event
952	content.
953	
954	The response is the updated execution state. Migrating a `completed` or
955	`terminated` execution returns `409 conflict` and changes nothing. A missing
956	execution or a target version that does not exist for the workflow returns
957	`404 not_found`; a cross-tenant reference is the same missing resource. A
958	missing or mistyped `version`, an unknown field, or a non-finite number is a
959	`400 validation_error`. Migrating a running execution to the version it is
960	already bound to returns the current state as-is, appending no event and
961	writing no checkpoint; a `completed` or `terminated` execution instead
962	returns `409 conflict` even when the target version is exactly the one it is
963	bound to. Reusing an idempotency key for another operation is a `409
964	conflict`. The migration event is listed directly by the per-execution
965	events query, and node outputs produced after the migration belong to the
966	target version's definition. Approver-list validation, lease renewal, and
967	delivery history keep their existing semantics before and after a migration.

969	### Start an execution

971	```http

976	```
977	
978	Returns HTTP 201. The execution starts in `running` state. Without an
979	explicit `version`, it binds to the workflow's current version at start time;

981	`404 not_found`). See "Workflow versions" for the binding and upgrade rules.

983	An execution may declare a timeout:
984

987	```

989	`timeout_seconds` is a positive number of seconds counted from the moment the

993	
994	An execution may also declare its own webhook `subscriptions`, which apply in
995	addition to the ones its workflow declares:
996	
997	```json
998	{
999	  "id": "run-3",
1000	  "workflow_id": "order-flow",
1001	  "input": {},
1002	  "subscriptions": [{"url": "https://hooks.example.com/ops", "events": ["node_completed"], "max_attempts": 3}]
1003	}
1004	```

1006	### Inspect an execution
1007	
1008	```http
1009	GET /executions/run-1
1010	GET /executions/run-1/events
1011	GET /executions/run-1/checkpoints
1012	```
1013	
1014	The first endpoint returns the materialized state. The second returns the
1015	ordered event stream. The third returns the ordered checkpoints; each entry
1016	gives its `sequence`, the `event_sequence` position it was taken at, the full
1017	`state` summary, and `created_at`.

1019	### Webhook notifications
1020	
1021	Subscriptions declared on a workflow or an execution deliver outbound webhook
1022	messages when business events occur. Each webhook subscription contains exactly:
1023	
1024	- `url`: a non-empty `http` or `https` address to POST to;
1025	- `events`: a non-empty array of event types without duplicates, drawn from
1026	  `node_completed`, `execution_completed`, `execution_terminated`, and
1027	  `approval_decided` (a termination is the same event type whatever its
1028	  reason);
1029	- `timeout_seconds` (optional): a positive number of seconds to wait for each
1030	  delivery attempt, defaulting to 5;
1031	- `max_attempts` (optional): an integer between 1 and 10, defaulting to 1.
1032	
1033	Any other field, a missing `url` or `events`, a mistyped value, an empty or
1034	duplicated event list, an unknown event type, an empty or non-http(s) `url`,
1035	a non-finite number, a non-positive timeout or attempt count, or more than
1036	ten attempts is a 400 `validation_error` and rejects the whole request — no
1037	workflow, execution, or subscription is partially written. A subscription
1038	may instead declare a queue target (`queue` instead of `url`); see "Queue
1039	subscriptions" below.
1040	
1041	When a subscribed event occurs, a JSON message is POSTed to each matching
1042	target immediately: the body carries `event_type`, `execution_id`, and the
1043	event's details (such as `node_id` for a completed node or `approver` for an
1044	approval decision). Each delivery request carries an `Idempotency-Key`
1045	header; retries of the same event reuse the same key, and different events
1046	never share a key. A delivery is attempted at most the subscription's
1047	`max_attempts` times, with an increasing backoff between attempts. An
1048	unreachable target, a timeout, or a non-2xx response marks the attempt as
1049	failed, but a failed delivery never changes the outcome of the call that
1050	triggered it.
1051	
1052	Deliveries do not append execution events, do not add fields to the execution
1053	state, and are never triggered by replay, recovery, or queries, so
1054	checkpoints and replay conclusions are unaffected. An execution that declares
1055	no subscriptions keeps exactly the same state, event stream, and advancement
1056	results as before.
1057	
1058	### Inspect the delivery history
1059	
1060	```http
1061	GET /executions/run-1/deliveries
1062	```
1063	
1064	Returns `{"deliveries": [...]}` in the order the events occurred. Each record
1065	gives its `sequence`, the subscription `url`, the `event_type`, the
1066	`event_sequence` that triggered it, the delivery `idempotency_key`, the final
1067	`status` (`delivered` or `failed`), the `attempt_count`, an `attempts` list
1068	recording each try's `status_code` or `error` (so a retry that eventually
1069	succeeds is visible attempt by attempt), and `occurred_at`. Querying the
1070	history of a missing execution returns 404 `not_found` and records nothing.
1071	Every delivery attempt is recorded, including one whose history record itself
1072	could not be written: such a failure is not swallowed — it is retried once in
1073	a fresh write carrying `status` `failed` and a `persistence_error` describing
1074	the write failure, so the attempt remains visible whenever the database can
1075	accept it (and is logged rather than silently dropped if it cannot).
1076	
1077	### Queue subscriptions
1078	
1079	A subscription may declare a queue target instead of a webhook `url`:
1080	
1081	```json
1082	{
1083	  "id": "run-4",
1084	  "workflow_id": "order-flow",
1085	  "input": {},
1086	  "subscriptions": [{"queue": "order-events", "events": ["node_completed"], "visibility_seconds": 60}]
1087	}
1088	```
1089	
1090	A queue subscription contains exactly:
1091	
1092	- `queue`: a non-empty queue name of any length;
1093	- `events`: the same non-empty event-type list a webhook subscription takes;
1094	- `visibility_seconds` (optional): a positive number of seconds a pulled
1095	  message stays invisible while awaiting acknowledgement, defaulting to 30.
1096	
1097	Exactly one of `url` and `queue` must be present in a subscription. Any
1098	other field, a missing or invalid `events` list, an empty queue name, or a
1099	non-positive or non-finite visibility timeout is a 400 `validation_error`
1100	that rejects the whole request without partial writes. Queue names are
1101	unique per tenant across declarations: declaring a name that another
1102	workflow or execution of the same tenant already declared is a 409
1103	`conflict`, while different tenants may reuse the same names freely.
1104	
1105	A workflow or an execution may declare several queue targets. Every
1106	execution gets its own queues — those declared on the workflow revision it
1107	is bound to, plus those it declares itself — and when a subscribed event
1108	occurs, a message carrying the event type and its details is appended to
1109	each matching queue of that execution, in occurrence order. The append is
1110	atomic with the event itself: a rejected operation leaves no queued message
1111	behind. Each message carries an idempotency key that is deterministic per
1112	event and queue: every delivery of the same message reuses the same key,
1113	and different events never share a key. Queues add no fields to the
1114	execution state and append no events, and replay, recovery, and queries
1115	never enqueue. Executions that declare no queue targets behave exactly as
1116	before.
1117	
1118	### Inspect the queue state
1119	
1120	```http
1121	GET /executions/run-4/queues
1122	X-Tenant-Id: acme
1123	```
1124	
1125	Returns `{"queues": [...]}` with one entry per queue of the execution, in
1126	declaration order; an execution with no queue targets gets the definite
1127	empty result `{"queues": []}`. Each entry gives its `queue` name, the
1128	`visibility_seconds` in effect, and the queue's `messages` in entry order —
1129	an empty list for a queue that never received a message. Each message record
1130	gives its `sequence` (the entry order), the `event_type` and
1131	`event_sequence` that produced it, the event `payload`, the message
1132	`idempotency_key`, the `delivery_count`, a `deliveries` list recording every
1133	delivery with its `delivery` number and `delivered_at` time, the
1134	`enqueued_at` time, and the current `status` (`pending`, `delivered`, or
1135	`acknowledged`). Querying the queues of a missing execution — including one
1136	owned by another tenant — is the usual 404 `not_found`.
1137	
1138	### Pull messages from a queue
1139	
1140	```http
1141	POST /executions/run-4/queues/order-events/pull
1142	Idempotency-Key: pull-request-1
1143	X-Tenant-Id: acme
1144	
1145	{}
1146	```
1147	
1148	The body must be an empty object. The response is `{"messages": [...]}`: the
1149	currently pending messages in entry order, each rendered like the message
1150	records of the queue state query. A pulled message becomes invisible for the
1151	queue's visibility timeout; if it is not acknowledged by then, it returns to
1152	the pending set and is delivered again — the queue semantics are at least
1153	once, and every delivery is recorded in the message's delivery history.
1154	Pulling an empty queue, or one whose messages are all invisible, is a
1155	definite empty result `{"messages": []}`, not an error. Every delivery to
1156	the caller is metered as one `delivery_attempted` usage record, exactly like
1157	an outbound webhook attempt, and counts toward the tenant's bill.
1158	
1159	### Acknowledge a message
1160	
1161	```http
1162	POST /executions/run-4/queues/order-events/ack
1163	Idempotency-Key: ack-request-1
1164	X-Tenant-Id: acme
1165	
1166	{"idempotency_key": "run-4:2:queue:order-events"}
1167	```
1168	
1169	The body must contain exactly `idempotency_key`, naming a message of the
1170	queue. Acknowledgement is explicit and final: the message permanently leaves
1171	the queue and is never delivered again, and the response is
1172	`{"acknowledged": true}`. Acknowledging a message that was already
1173	acknowledged, or a key the queue does not know, is a 404 `not_found`.
1174	Pulling from or acknowledging a queue the execution does not have, or one
1175	belonging to a missing or cross-tenant execution, is likewise a 404
1176	`not_found`. Pull and acknowledge are idempotent commands like every other
1177	operation: repeating one with the same `Idempotency-Key` returns the
1178	original result, and reusing a key across different operations is a 409
1179	`conflict`.

1181	### Schedules
1182	
1183	A workflow may declare a schedule so the service creates executions
1184	automatically. The declaration happens at workflow creation (a `schedule`
1185	field next to `id` and `nodes`) or later through the update endpoint, and it
1186	takes effect from the moment it is stored. A schedule contains exactly:
1187	
1188	- `interval_seconds`: a positive integer number of seconds between runs —
1189	  or, alternatively, `cron`: a five-field cron expression (`minute hour
1190	  day-of-month month day-of-week`) whose fields support `*`, `*/step`,
1191	  single values, ranges `a-b`, ranges with steps `a-b/step`, and
1192	  comma-separated lists, with 0 and 7 both meaning Sunday. Exactly one of
1193	  `interval_seconds` and `cron` must be present;
1194	- `input`: the object used as the execution input of every created run;
1195	- `missed_policy`: either `catch_up` or `skip`.
1196	
1197	Whenever a period of the plan comes due, the service creates one execution
1198	for the workflow with the declared input. The created execution is exactly a
1199	manually created one: it starts `running` with the same state shape and the
1200	usual `execution_started` event, and advancing, approvals, leases, retries,
1201	timeouts, and cancellation all behave identically. The trigger itself writes
1202	nothing into the created execution's event stream and adds no fields to its
1203	state; the schedule's own record of when it fired and which execution it
1204	created is exposed through the status query below.
1205	
1206	Creation is idempotent per schedule period: a repeated trigger or a repeated
1207	request for the same period returns the same execution and never creates a
1208	second one, under either missed policy. When periods were missed — the
1209	schedule was paused, or the service was not running — `catch_up` makes up
1210	exactly the single most recent missed period, while `skip` makes up none;
1211	neither policy ever creates more than one execution for the same period.
1212	
1213	An invalid declaration rejects the whole request with 400
1214	`validation_error` and writes nothing: a non-positive or non-integer
1215	`interval_seconds`, a cron expression with other than five fields, out-of
1216	range values, or unparseable fragments, declaring both `interval_seconds`
1217	and `cron`, a `missed_policy` other than `catch_up` or `skip`, a missing or
1218	mistyped `input`, or any unknown field.
1219	
1220	### Declare or replace a schedule
1221	
1222	```http
1223	PUT /workflows/nightly-orders/schedule
1224	Idempotency-Key: schedule-request-1
1225	
1226	{"interval_seconds":3600,"input":{"mode":"nightly"},"missed_policy":"catch_up"}
1227	```
1228	
1229	`POST` to the same path is accepted as well. The body is validated exactly
1230	like a schedule declared at creation time, and the response is the schedule
1231	status. Updating replaces the plan and re-anchors it at the update time; the
1232	paused flag is kept. A missing workflow returns 404 `not_found`, an invalid
1233	plan 400 `validation_error` with no partial write, and reusing an
1234	idempotency key from another operation is a 409 `conflict`.
1235	
1236	### Inspect the schedule status
1237	
1238	```http
1239	GET /workflows/nightly-orders/schedule
1240	```
1241	
1242	Returns a single `schedule` object with the status fields, or the definite
1243	empty result `{"schedule":null}` for a workflow that never declared a
1244	schedule. When a schedule exists the object is:
1245	
1246	```json
1247	{
1248	  "schedule": {"interval_seconds": 3600, "input": {"mode": "nightly"}, "missed_policy": "catch_up"},
1249	  "paused": false,
1250	  "last_triggered_at": "2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z",
1251	  "last_execution_id": "nightly-orders-scheduled-i:42"
1252	}

1254	
1255	The fields are:
1256	
1257	- `schedule`: the declared plan exactly as stored — either
1258	  `{"interval_seconds": <positive integer>, "input": <object>, "missed_policy": "catch_up"|"skip"}`
1259	  or `{"cron": "<five-field expression>", "input": <object>, "missed_policy": ...}`;
1260	  the input is the declared object verbatim;

1262	- `last_triggered_at`: an ISO-8601 UTC timestamp string ending in `Z`, or

1268	the first trigger. A missing workflow returns 404 `not_found`.

1270	### Pause and resume a schedule
1271	
1272	```http
1273	POST /workflows/nightly-orders/schedule/pause
1274	Idempotency-Key: pause-request-1
1275	
1276	{}
1277	```

1279	```http
1280	POST /workflows/nightly-orders/schedule/resume
1281	Idempotency-Key: resume-request-1
1282	
1283	{}

1286	Both bodies must be empty objects; a missing or mistyped body, an unknown
1287	field, or a non-finite number is a 400 `validation_error`. While paused, due
1288	periods create no executions. Resuming settles the periods that came due
1289	during the pause according to the missed policy: `catch_up` immediately
1290	creates the single most recent missed run, `skip` creates none. Pausing or
1291	resuming a workflow that has no schedule, or any schedule operation on a
1292	missing workflow, returns 404 `not_found`; reusing an idempotency key across
1293	operations returns 409 `conflict`. Both responses carry the schedule status.
1294	
1295	Workflows that declare no schedule are unaffected: their creation,
1296	advancement, approvals, deliveries, checkpoints, recovery, and replay behave
1297	exactly as before, with no additional fields or events.
